# Śiva, spelled the way the sources wrote it
There is a version of this name the early internet had to settle for: *shiva*. This is the file on how **Śiva** replaced it.

Śiva's mythology is among the most philosophically ambitious in the Sanskrit tradition. He is not merely a destroyer but the principle of transformation itself: the dancer whose final gesture dissolves a weary cosmos, the ascetic whose inner heat saves the gods from poison, and the householder whose marriage to the mountain-goddess reunites withdrawal and engagement. His stories move between Himalayan forest and cremation ground, bridal chamber and battlefield, teaching that creation and destruction are phases of a single rhythm. Every major strand of Hindu text — Vedic hymn, Upaniṣadic meditation, Purāṇic narrative, and Tamil devotional poetry — returns to him as both absolute beyond and intimate lord. Śiva's worship spread from the subcontinent to Southeast Asia, Tibet, and the diaspora, producing distinct regional forms. Tamil poets, Kashmiri philosophers, and Nepalese tantric communities all shaped his cult. Today he is one of the most widely recognized Hindu deities, his image meditating in bronze, stone, and film across the global Hindu world. When the gods and demons churned the cosmic ocean in search of amṛta, the elixir of immortality, the first thing to rise was not nectar but Halāhala, a poison black enough to scorch every world.  Creation began to suffocate.

That is the figure this file is about — and the temple now standing at its restored name.
## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Śiva
- **ASCII form:** shiva
- **Meaning:** "The auspicious one; the deity of destruction, transformation, and regeneration, the third member of the Hindu Trimūrti alongside Brahmā and Viṣṇu."
- **Domain of influence:** Destruction, Transformation, Dance
- **Pantheon:** Sanskrit
- **Classification:** Tier 1
- **Original script:** शिव
- **Series:** The Restoration Files, No. 222 of 271
## The Name Before the Marks

**Śiva** preserves its form without added diacritics: the restoration here is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form the tradition's own sources record. *shiva* and **Śiva** may look interchangeable to a search box; they are not interchangeable to a philologist.
## The Temple That Stands Now

The restored name is not a plaque; it is an address. The temple of **Śiva** lives at [/sites/shiva/](/sites/shiva/), with its mythology in the [lore halls](/sites/shiva/lore/), its peer-reviewed record in the [Scholarly Edition](/sites/shiva/scholars/), and its place in the pattern atlas on the [patterns floor](/sites/shiva/patterns/).

The restoration preserves more than the ASCII form can say — stress, length, or a letter the Latin keyboard lost — which places it in Tier-1: mechanically verifiable, information-rich.

Every flagship temple is hand-built to the same standard: the original script displayed with its provenance, the pronunciation reconstructed phoneme by phoneme, the sources named — because a restoration you cannot audit is just a spelling with confidence.
## The Archetype at Work

A temple is also a reading of what this figure *means* — and meanings have addresses in the modern world. The [pattern atlas](/patterns/) maps **Śiva** to the industries its archetype genuinely resonates with, each match argued, weighted, and open to challenge:

- **Music, Arts & Performance** — Naṭarāja, lord of the cosmic dance.
- **Yoga, Meditation & Holistic Wellness** — Adiyogi, the first yogi; modern yoga traces its lineage to him.
- **Disaster Resilience & Recovery** — Destruction as transformation; the rebuild after the fall.

The mapping is conservative on purpose: only resonances that can be argued aloud. The rest of the atlas follows the same rule, industry by industry.
## In the Sacred Texts

The Sanskrit tradition is not a vibe; it is a library. The [Sacred Texts collection](/texts/) holds [Rig Veda](/texts/rig-veda/) and [Ramayana](/texts/ramayana/) — the primary sources the temple's scholarship is built on, free to read, cross-linked back to the names they mention. The temple is the argument; the texts are the evidence.
